blocks.title: Features (Laxmikanth)
items: Some rights are for citizens only; others are for all persons (including foreigners and legal persons such as companies)

They are not absolute but qualified: the State may impose reasonable restrictions on them. Parliament (the legislature) imposes these limits, not the Supreme Court; the courts only decide whether a restriction is reasonable
They are available against the State; a few are also available against private persons (Art 15(2), Art 17, Art 23, Art 24)

Some are negative (they stop the State from doing something); some are positive (they require the State to do something, for example the Art 21A duty to provide education). One right can involve both kinds of duty
They are justiciable (enforceable in courts)
They are guaranteed and defended by the Supreme Court; a person whose right is violated can go directly to the Supreme Court

They are not sacrosanct (not beyond change): Parliament can curtail them, but only by a constitutional amendment under Art 368 passed by special majority (two-thirds of members present and voting, plus a majority of total membership, in each House; approval by the States is not needed), and the amendment must not destroy the basic structure of the Constitution (its core features, as laid down by the Supreme Court)
They can be suspended during a National Emergency, except Art 20 and Art 21. Art 19 is suspended automatically only when the Emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression

They are limited by Art 31A, Art 31B and Art 31C (saving of certain laws); by Art 33 (Parliament can restrict rights of the armed forces and similar forces); by Art 34 (restriction while martial law — military rule — is in force); and by Art 35 (only Parliament, not State legislatures, can make laws on certain Fundamental Rights)
Most are self-executory (they work directly, without needing a separate law to bring them into force)

blocks.title: Why 'fundamental' / purpose
items: They are granted, guaranteed and protected by the Constitution, which is the fundamental (supreme) law of the country
They are essential for the all-round development of the individual — material, intellectual, moral and spiritual
Fundamental Rights promote POLITICAL democracy, while the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) aim at social and economic democracy

They prevent tyranny by the executive and arbitrary laws by the legislature, ensuring 'a government of laws and not of men' (rule of law). They also protect people against a party that simply has an electoral majority
They are described as both natural rights and legal rights. Their main job is to protect individuals and minorities against arbitrary action by the State

Significance: they are the bedrock (foundation) of democracy and the bulwark (protective wall) of liberty; they uphold the rule of law; they protect minorities; they strengthen the secular fabric; they protect human dignity; they allow participation in public life (through expression, association and movement); and they build unity by accommodating diversity

items.what: Magna Carta (England)
items.detail: A charter issued by King John under pressure from his barons (nobles). It was written in Latin and limited the king's authority. It was the first written document on rights, but it was not a charter of equal rights for everyone

items.what: English Bill of Rights
items.detail: An Act of the English Parliament that limited the powers of the Crown (the monarch). It became a model for later rights documents, including the US Bill of Rights

items.what: US Bill of Rights
items.detail: The first 10 amendments to the US Constitution. It inspired India's Part III, but India did not copy it word for word. The US 5th and 14th Amendments have 'due process of law' clauses (courts check whether the law itself is fair), whereas India's Art 21 says 'procedure established by law'

items.what: Commonwealth of India Bill
items.detail: Drafted by the National Convention, chaired by Tej Bahadur Sapru, with Annie Besant and colleagues. George Lansbury presented it in the British House of Commons in December 1925, but it failed at the first reading. Its Section 7 listed SEVEN fundamental rights, including free elementary education

items.what: Nehru Report
items.detail: Included a list of fundamental rights

items.what: Karachi session of Congress
items.detail: Presided over by Vallabhbhai Patel. It passed a resolution on Fundamental Rights and economic policy that went beyond civil liberties, including a living wage and free primary education

items.what: Advisory Committee constituted
items.detail: The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas, chaired by Sardar Patel. Its Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee was chaired by J.B. Kripalani

head: Idea
Meaning

blocks.title: Key facts
items: The 44th Amendment (1978, passed under the Janata Government, not Congress) omitted Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31. So Art 19(1) now has 6 freedoms (originally 7)
The Right to Property did NOT become a Directive Principle. Art 301 deals with trade and commerce, not property
Amendments made because of property disputes: 1st, 4th, 17th, 25th, 39th, 40th and 42nd

Compensation is still guaranteed in Part III in two cases: (1) property of a minority educational institution — Art 30(1A), added by the 44th Amendment; (2) land a person cultivates himself, within the ceiling limit — market-value compensation under the second proviso of Art 31A, added by the 17th Amendment, 1964

Eminent domain means the State's sovereign power to take private property for public use without the owner's consent. The safeguards are: it must be for a public purpose, and compensation must be paid

Art 300A includes seven procedural sub-rights (Supreme Court in Kolkata Municipal Corporation v Bimal Kumar Shah, 16 May 2024): (1) notice, (2) hearing, (3) a reasoned decision, (4) acquisition only for a public purpose, (5) restitution or fair compensation, (6) an efficient and quick process, (7) conclusion of the process (taking possession)
Art 265: no tax can be collected except by authority of law (a government circular alone cannot levy a tax)

head: Article
Added by
Protects
rows: 1st Amendment, 1951 (scope widened by the 4th and 17th Amendments)

Protects 5 categories of laws from challenge under Art 14 and Art 19: (1) acquisition of estates; (2) the State taking over management of property; (3) amalgamation (merger) of corporations; (4) changing the rights of directors or shareholders; (5) ending or changing mining leases (including mineral oil). Such laws need not be placed in the Ninth Schedule
1st Amendment, 1951 (added together with the Ninth Schedule)

Protects laws placed in the Ninth Schedule from challenge under ANY Fundamental Right (so it is wider than Art 31A). It shields only against Part III — it does not save a law that the legislature had no power to make. Laws added after 24 April 1973 can be reviewed for violating the basic structure (Waman Rao case 1980; I.R. Coelho case 2007)
25th Amendment, 1971

Protects laws made to implement Art 39(b) and Art 39(c) (fair distribution of material resources, and preventing concentration of wealth) from challenge under Art 14 and Art 19. The clause that stopped courts from questioning the law's 'declaration' (that it gives effect to these principles) was struck down in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973). The 42nd Amendment's extension of Art 31C to all Directive Principles was struck down in the Minerva Mills case (1980); the rest of the 42nd Amendment survived

subcards.title: Art 12–13: 'State' and judicial review
subcards.summary: Who counts as 'State' under Article 12, and why laws that violate Fundamental Rights are void under Article 13.
at_a_glance: Article 12 (definition of 'State') and Article 13 (laws against Fundamental Rights are void)
The definition applies to Part III (Fundamental Rights) 'unless the context otherwise requires'. Article 36 applies the same definition to Part IV (Directive Principles).
Art 13(1) covers laws made before the Constitution; Art 13(2) covers laws made after it. In both cases only the part that conflicts with Fundamental Rights is void.
Acts, Ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and customs or usages that have the force of law
A Constitutional Amendment is not 'law' under Art 13. The 24th Amendment (1971) inserted Art 13(4) and Art 368(3) to say this.

Severability (only the bad part of a law is cut off), Eclipse (an old law sleeps instead of dying), Non-waiver (rights cannot be given up); Prospective overruling (a new ruling applies only to the future) is also studied with these

Judicial review is the courts' power to check laws and strike down those against the Constitution. The phrase 'judicial review' is not used anywhere in the Constitution; the power comes from Art 13, Art 32 and Art 226.
Ajay Hasia (1981), Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002), Golak Nath (1967), Kesavananda (1973)

blocks.title: Art 12 — 'State' includes (inclusive definition)
head: Category
Examples
rows: Government and Parliament of India
The Union executive and the Union legislature (Parliament)
Government and Legislature of each State
The State executive and the State legislature
All local authorities
Municipalities, panchayats, district boards and improvement trusts. These are local bodies created by law (statutory); they need not be a government department to count as 'State'.
Other authorities (within India, or under the control of the Government of India)
Bodies created by law (statutory) or not created by law (non-statutory), for example LIC, ONGC and SAIL. Even a private body can be 'State' if it works as an instrument or agency of the State.
blocks.note: NOT 'State': foreign embassies in India, and purely private persons or companies. Courts are NOT named in Art 12, so whether the judiciary is an 'other authority' is the well-known unclear point.

blocks.title: Why Art 12 is 'comprehensive yet ambiguous'
items: The definition is inclusive (it says 'includes'), not exhaustive — so bodies not listed can also be 'State'.
The Constitution does not define 'other authorities'; its meaning has been filled in by a series of court decisions.
The definition applies to Part III 'unless the context otherwise requires'. So it is not a fixed rule for every place the word 'State' appears in the Constitution.

Fundamental Rights are mostly claimed against the State. Some can also be claimed against private individuals (Art 15(2), Art 17, Art 23, Art 24) — see Right to Equality and Right against Exploitation.

blocks.title: Clauses of Art 13
head: Clause
Content
rows: Laws in force before the Constitution, inconsistent with Part III, are void TO THE EXTENT of inconsistency
The State shall not make any law that TAKES AWAY or ABRIDGES (reduces) Part III rights. A law that breaks this rule is void to the extent it breaks it.
'Law' includes Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law
'Laws in force' means laws passed by a competent authority before the Constitution began and not repealed, even if they were not then in operation at all, or not in operation in some areas
Nothing in Art 13 applies to a Constitutional Amendment made under Art 368 (clause added by the 24th Amendment, 1971)

children.label: Permanent laws — Acts of Parliament and of State Legislatures
Temporary laws — Ordinances issued by the President and by Governors
Delegated legislation (rules made by the executive under an Act) — orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications
Non-legislative sources — a custom or usage HAVING THE FORCE OF LAW (not every social custom)

blocks.title: Consequences
items: Courts can review delegated legislation on two grounds: going beyond the powers given by the parent Act (ultra vires) and violating Fundamental Rights.

An Ordinance cannot abridge or take away Fundamental Rights — it has the same limits as an Act. An Ordinance can amend or repeal a Central Act and can be retrospective (apply to the past). But it cannot amend the Constitution.
'Void to the extent of inconsistency' means only the conflicting part is legally invalid; the Constitution itself is not changed.

Art 13 protects only Fundamental Rights (Part III). A law that conflicts only with a Directive Principle of State Policy (for example Art 43) cannot be struck down, because Art 37 makes Directive Principles non-justiciable (not enforceable in court).

blocks.title: Doctrines at a glance
head: Doctrine
Meaning
Key cases
rows: Severability (separability)

Only the offending part is void; the valid part survives if it can be separated. Test: would the legislature have passed the remaining part on its own? If the parts cannot be separated, form one single scheme, or too little is left, the whole law falls.

A.K. Gopalan (1950): Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act 1950 (which barred telling the court the grounds of detention) was struck down, the rest stayed valid. Also F.N. Balsara (1951); R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla (1957); Minerva Mills (1980); Kihoto Hollohan (1992): paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule was struck down.
Eclipse

A pre-Constitution law that conflicts with a Fundamental Right is not dead but dormant (eclipsed — under a shadow). It comes back to life if the Fundamental Right is amended to remove the conflict. Even while eclipsed, it stays valid for past transactions, for rights and liabilities that arose before 1950, and for non-citizens.

Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955): the 1st Amendment changed Art 19(6), so the Motor Vehicles law revived. Deep Chand (1959) and Mahendra Lal Jain (1962): eclipse does not apply to post-Constitution laws — they are still-born (void from birth). Ambica Mills (1974): a post-Constitution law violating Art 19 is still valid against non-citizens. Dulare Lodh (1984): eclipse applied even against citizens.
Waiver (non-waiver in India)
A person cannot waive (give up) Fundamental Rights, because they are a matter of public policy, not just a personal benefit. (The USA allows waiver.)

Behram Khurshid Pesikaka (1954); Basheshar Nath (1958): Art 14 rights cannot be given up by agreement; Olga Tellis (1985): no estoppel against the Constitution (a person's earlier statement or conduct cannot stop him from claiming a constitutional right); Nar Singh Pal (2000)
Prospective overruling

The new ruling applies only to the future; past decisions are left valid. The doctrine comes from the USA. It was first applied in India in Golak Nath (1967), where the 1st, 4th and 17th Amendments were left valid.
Golak Nath (1967)

blocks.title: Is an amendment 'law' under Art 13?
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Shankari Prasad (1951)
Upheld the 1st Amendment. An amendment made under constituent power (the power to amend the Constitution) is not 'law' under Art 13, so Fundamental Rights can be amended.
Separates ordinary law-making from constituent (amending) power
Sajjan Singh (1964)
Followed Shankari Prasad and upheld the 17th Amendment. Justice Mudholkar asked whether the basic features of the Constitution can be changed.
First seed of the basic structure idea (some core features of the Constitution cannot be changed even by amendment)
Golak Nath (1967, 11 judges)
An amendment IS 'law' under Art 13(2), so Parliament cannot take away or abridge Fundamental Rights. The court used prospective overruling.
Led to the 24th Amendment
Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges, 7:6, Chief Justice S.M. Sikri)
Upheld the 24th Amendment. Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights but cannot change the basic structure (the core features of the Constitution).
Overruled Golak Nath and created the basic structure doctrine
Minerva Mills (1980)
The limited nature of the amending power is itself a basic feature. Struck down Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment.
Parliament cannot turn its limited amending power into an unlimited power
L. Chandra Kumar (1997)
Judicial review by High Courts (Art 226) and the Supreme Court (Art 32) is part of the basic structure; tribunals cannot fully take it away
Tribunals add to the courts; they do not replace them

blocks.title: Amendments
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. Inserted Art 13(4) and Art 368(3) (an amendment is not 'law'). The President SHALL (must) give assent to an amendment bill.
Inserted Art 226A — High Courts were barred from examining the validity of Central laws
Omitted Art 226A — High Courts' power of review was restored

blocks.title: Amendment procedure for Part III
items: Amending only a Fundamental Right needs a special majority in each House of Parliament (a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting). NO ratification (approval) by the States is needed, because Fundamental Rights are not listed in the proviso to Art 368(2).

Forming new States (Art 4) needs only a simple majority. Changing the Election of the President needs a special majority and ratification by half the States. The basic structure cannot be destroyed even by an amendment.
Even though amendments are kept out of Art 13, an amendment still CANNOT destroy the basic structure.
The phrase 'judicial review' is used nowhere in the Constitution, and the Constitution does not define 'basic structure'.
Art 13 is the source of judicial review of laws (Laxmikanth says it 'expressively provides for' it). The Supreme Court exercises it through Art 32, and High Courts through Art 226.
A law can be struck down on three grounds: it infringes Fundamental Rights; it is outside the competence (power) of the authority that made it; or it is repugnant to (against) the Constitution.
Other Articles that support judicial review: Art 131, Art 132–136, Art 143, Art 227, Art 245, Art 246, Art 251, Art 254, Art 372.
A High Court, under Art 226, can examine whether a Constitutional Amendment is valid.

subcards.title: Right to Equality (Art 14–18)
subcards.summary: Articles 14 to 18 give five equality rights: equality before law (Art 14), no discrimination by the State (Art 15), equal chance in government jobs (Art 16), abolition of untouchability (Art 17) and abolition of titles (Art 18).
at_a_glance: Available to all persons — citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies
Apply against private persons too, not only against the State
Indra Sawhney case (1992) — upheld 27% OBC (Other Backward Classes) reservation, required the 'creamy layer' (better-off OBCs) to be excluded, and capped total reservation at 50%
Art 17 and Art 18 secure social equality
Related Articles: Art 39(d), Art 46, Art 330, Art 332, Art 335, Art 340, Art 341, Art 342A

sections.heading: Art 14 — Equality before law and Rule of Law

blocks.text: Art 14: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. 'Person' includes legal persons (companies, statutory corporations, societies).

blocks.title: Two ideas in Art 14
head: Aspect
Equality before law
Equal protection of laws
rows: Origin
British
American
Nature
Negative concept (says what must NOT happen — no special privileges)
Positive concept (requires the State to treat equals equally)
Means
No special privileges for anyone. Everyone is equally subject to the ordinary law and the ordinary courts. No one is above the law.
Equal treatment in equal circumstances: people in the same situation get the same law, so like are treated alike. It does NOT mean one same law for everyone regardless of their differences.

blocks.title: Reasonable classification
items: Art 14 forbids class legislation (a law that favours or targets a group without good reason) but permits reasonable classification (grouping people on a sensible basis) — Anwar Ali Sarkar case (1952).

A classification is valid only if it passes two separate tests: (1) intelligible differentia — a clear, understandable difference between the grouped and the left-out people; AND (2) rational nexus — that difference must be logically connected to the purpose of the law. A visible difference alone is not enough.
Valid examples: minors versus adults; small versus large industries; literate versus illiterate persons for a job that needs reading; flood-hit areas chosen for relief.
A law that gives the executive (government officers) unguided, uncontrolled discretion — power to choose without any rules — violates Art 14.
Even a law aimed at a single person or company (a 'class of one') can be valid in exceptional circumstances — Chiranjit Lal case (1950).

Arbitrariness (acting without reason) is the opposite of equality — E.P. Royappa case (1974). A law can be struck down as 'manifestly arbitrary' (clearly unreasonable) even if it makes no classification at all — Shayara Bano case (2017).

blocks.title: Rule of Law (A.V. Dicey, British jurist)
head: Element
Applies in India?
rows: 1. Absence of arbitrary power — no one can be punished except for a clear breach of law
Yes
2. Equality before law — everyone, rich or poor, official or ordinary citizen, is subject to the ordinary law and the ordinary courts
Yes
3. Primacy of individual rights — the constitution is the result of rights already held by people, not their source
No (in India the Constitution is the source of rights)
blocks.note: Main features of Rule of Law: limits on government power, equality before law, and liberty and civil rights. Discretion is still allowed if it stays within the law — used reasonably, for the purpose the law allows, on relevant grounds. Rule of Law in Art 14 is a basic feature of the Constitution — Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975). WJP (World Justice Project) Rule of Law Index 2025: India ranked 86th of 143 countries; 2026 edition (released 21 Oct 2026): India 88th of 143 (as of Nov 2026).

blocks.title: Exceptions to equality
head: Who / what
Protection
rows: President and Governor (Art 361)

Not answerable to any court for official acts. During the term of office: no criminal case can be started, and no order of arrest or imprisonment can be issued. A civil suit for personal acts is allowed only after 2 months' written notice (so it is not permanently barred). The Government of India or the State Government can still be sued.
Newspaper, radio and TV (Art 361A)
Cannot be sued or punished for publishing a substantially true report of proceedings in Parliament or a State Legislature
MPs (Art 105(2))
No court case against an MP for anything said or any vote given in Parliament or its committees
MLAs (Art 194(2))
Same protection for MLAs, for anything said or any vote given in the State Legislature
Art 31C

Laws made to give effect to Art 39(b) or Art 39(c) (fair distribution of material resources; preventing concentration of wealth) cannot be challenged under Art 14 — only these two. Hence the saying 'where Art 31C comes in, Art 14 goes out'.
Foreign heads of State (sovereigns), ambassadors and diplomats
Immunity (protection) from civil and criminal cases in Indian courts
United Nations (UNO) and its agencies
Enjoy diplomatic immunity (cannot be sued in Indian courts)
blocks.note: Chief Ministers do NOT get any such immunity.

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri case (1950)
A law that dealt with only one company was upheld
Even a 'class of one' (a single company) can be a reasonable classification
Anwar Ali Sarkar case (1952)
A law letting the government send any case it chose to special courts, without guidelines, was struck down
Laid down the reasonable-classification test; unguided discretion given to the executive violates Art 14
Basheshar Nath case (1958)
Fundamental Rights (here Art 14) cannot be waived (given up), even by a person's own voluntary tax settlement
Doctrine of non-waiver (a person cannot give up a Fundamental Right) — see Art 12–13 card
A.K. Kraipak case (1969)
A selection board member who was also a candidate for the same post — this is bias
Rules of natural justice (fair hearing, no bias) — though not written in Art 14 — apply to administrative action too
Bennett Coleman case (1972)
Government limits on newsprint and number of pages of newspapers violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 14
E.P. Royappa case (1974)
Equality is a dynamic (wide, changing) concept; arbitrariness is its opposite
Gave a new dimension to Art 14 — arbitrary action is itself unequal
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
Rule of Law in Art 14 is part of the basic structure of the Constitution
Maneka Gandhi case (1978)

The procedure for taking away life or liberty under Art 21 must be fair, just and reasonable. Art 14, Art 19 and Art 21 are linked, not separate — the 'golden triangle'. In that case, a hearing given after the decision (post-decisional hearing) was accepted.
See the Right to Freedom card
Vishaka case (1997)
Supreme Court laid down guidelines against sexual harassment of women at the workplace, based on Art 14, Art 15, Art 19 and Art 21
NALSA case (2014)
Transgender persons may declare their own gender (no surgery needed). The Centre and the States must treat them as socially and educationally backward classes for reservation.
Shayara Bano case (2017)

Talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) was set aside by a 3:2 majority. The majority judges gave different reasons: Justices Nariman and Lalit said it is manifestly arbitrary under Art 14; Justice Joseph said it is against religious law itself.
Established the 'manifest arbitrariness' test (a law clearly unreasonable can be struck down under Art 14)

blocks.title: Meaning of equality
items: Equality and liberty are the two most essential rights in a democracy. Equality means no one has special privileges.
Signs that equality is absent: the caste system, gender discrimination, and absence of rule of law.

Social equality: Art 17 and Art 18 (also Art 15). Political equality: Art 325 and Art 326 (adult suffrage — every adult can vote). Economic equality: Art 39 (for example, Art 39(d) — equal pay for equal work for men and women).
Complete equality of men and women is guaranteed by Art 14 and Art 15.

Political equality alone does not bring social and economic equality. Ambedkar warned that on 26 Jan 1950 India would 'enter a life of contradictions' — equal in politics, unequal in social and economic life.
Indian equality is substantive (real equality, not just equal rules on paper): justified reservation helps achieve equality, as long as it stays within constitutional limits.

sections.heading: Art 15 — No discrimination and special provisions

blocks.title: Clauses of Art 15 (citizens only)
head: Clause
Provision
rows: The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds ONLY of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. ('Descent' and 'residence' are NOT in this list.) The word 'only' means other grounds are not barred — but adding a false extra reason does not save a discrimination that is really based on these grounds.

No citizen can be barred, on these grounds, from: (a) shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment — whether or not the State funds them; (b) wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort that are maintained wholly or partly by State funds OR dedicated to the general public. This clause binds both the State AND private persons.
The State may make special provisions for women and children (for example, reserved seats for women in local bodies)
Special provisions for SEBCs (socially and educationally backward classes) or for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes — added by the 1st Amendment, 1951

Special provisions for these classes in admission to educational institutions, including private institutions (aided or unaided), but NOT minority institutions under Art 30(1) — added by the 93rd Amendment, 2005. It is only enabling: it allows the State to act but does not force it.

(a) Special provisions for EWS (economically weaker sections) — those not already covered under clauses 15(4) and 15(5); (b) up to 10% seats for EWS in admissions, including private institutions, but not minority institutions — added by the 103rd Amendment, 2019
blocks.note: Art 15 has no enabling clause for senior citizens or aged persons. Example: asking a person to leave a cinema hall because of caste or status violates Art 15(2).

blocks.title: Art 15 cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
The Madras government's Communal G.O. (Government Order fixing college seats by caste and religion) violated Art 29(2). Directive Principles (here Art 46) cannot override Fundamental Rights.
Led to the 1st Amendment inserting Art 15(4)
M.R. Balaji case (1962)
Caste can be one factor but not the only test of backwardness — poverty, occupation and place of living also count. Reservation should generally be below 50%.
P.A. Inamdar case (2005)

The State cannot impose reservation quotas on unaided professional colleges, whether minority or non-minority. But the State can regulate them to stop capitation fees (donations for seats) and profiteering.
Led to the 93rd Amendment inserting Art 15(5)
Ashoka Kumar Thakur case (2008)

Upheld the 93rd Amendment and the 27% OBC quota in central educational institutions, with the creamy layer excluded. Whether it validly applies to private unaided institutions was left open (not decided).

blocks.title: Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006
items: Reservation in central higher educational institutions (such as IITs and IIMs): Scheduled Castes 15%, Scheduled Tribes 7.5%, OBCs 27%.
Upheld in April 2008 in the Ashoka Kumar Thakur case; the creamy layer must be excluded.
It does not automatically apply to every private college — the Act has its own definitions and exemptions.

blocks.title: Clauses of Art 16 (citizens only)
head: Clause
Provision
rows: Equality of opportunity for all citizens in employment or appointment to any office under the State
No discrimination in government jobs on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, DESCENT, place of birth or RESIDENCE (descent and residence are extra compared to Art 15(1))

Only PARLIAMENT (not a State legislature) may make residence a condition for jobs in a State, Union Territory or local authority. The Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act 1957 expired in 1974; such residence rules now exist only for Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. A.V.S. Narasimha Rao case (1969): the residence unit must be the whole State or UT, not a part of it. Separately, under Art 371D (added by the 32nd Amendment, 1973), the PRESIDENT by order can provide equitable job and education opportunities for different parts of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
The State may reserve posts for any 'backward class of citizens' that, in the State's opinion, is not adequately represented in State services. The text itself fixes no percentage limit.

Reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes — added by the 77th Amendment, 1995. The 85th Amendment, 2001 added 'consequential seniority' (an SC/ST employee promoted through reservation also keeps the seniority that comes with it), with effect from June 1995.

Reserved vacancies left unfilled in earlier years and carried forward are treated as a separate class. They are not added to the current year's vacancies when applying the 50% ceiling — added by the 81st Amendment, 2000.

A law may require that the office-holder or governing-body member of a religious or denominational institution must belong to that religion. (This does NOT allow ordinary government departments to recruit by religion.)
Up to 10% posts for EWS (economically weaker sections), excluding classes already covered under Art 16(4), in addition to existing reservation — added by the 103rd Amendment, 2019
blocks.note: Art 15(4) uses the words 'socially and educationally backward classes'; Art 16(4) uses 'backward class of citizens' — the two are not identical. The Constitution does not define 'backward classes'. Art 335: SC/ST claims to jobs must be considered consistently with efficiency of administration; a proviso added by the 82nd Amendment, 2000 allows relaxed qualifying marks or lower evaluation standards for SC/ST in promotion. Art 330 and Art 332: reserved seats for SC/ST in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies. Art 341: the President specifies the Scheduled Castes, and only Parliament can change the list. Art 340: commission to investigate backward classes (OBC welfare).

Mandal Commission report submitted: identified 3,743 castes (about 52% of the population) as backward, using 11 indicators (social, educational, economic); recommended 27% reservation for OBCs

Narasimha Rao government amended the OM: preference to poorer sections among OBCs, and an extra 10% for economically backward people not covered by any existing reservation
Supreme Court judgment in the Indra Sawhney (Mandal) case

76th Amendment — Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation Act placed in the Ninth Schedule (to protect it from court challenge)

Justice G. Rohini Commission set up (under Art 340) to examine sub-categorisation (dividing into sub-groups) of the central OBC list; its recommendations are not binding

105th Amendment — inserted Art 342A(3): States and UTs can again prepare their own SEBC lists, and need not consult the NCBC for them. The Central list can be changed only by a law of Parliament.

blocks.title: Indra Sawhney case (1992) — conditions
items: 27% OBC reservation was upheld; the 10% economic quota (clause (ii) of the 1991 OM) was struck down.
The 'poorer sections' preference was read to mean preference to the socially more backward among OBCs (poverty used as a measure of social backwardness).
The creamy layer (socially advanced, better-off OBCs) must be excluded — belonging to an OBC caste alone is not enough to get reservation.
No reservation in promotions (existing promotion quotas could continue for 5 years, up to 1997).
Total reservation must not exceed 50%, except in extraordinary situations. Carrying forward unfilled vacancies is valid, but within the 50% limit.

A permanent statutory body must be set up to hear complaints of wrong inclusion or exclusion in backward-class lists. As a result, the NCBC was set up in 1993, and State Backward Classes Commissions (including in AP) were also set up.
No relaxation of standards in promotion, because Art 335 requires efficiency of administration.

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters

'Catch-up rule': a senior general-category employee who is promoted later than a junior SC/ST employee regains his seniority over him
Nullified for SC/ST employees by the 85th Amendment

Removed the requirement (from Nagaraj) of quantifiable data showing SC/ST backwardness. Data on inadequate representation in the cadre is still needed. The creamy-layer principle applies to SC/ST in promotions.
Excluding the creamy layer does not remove that caste from the President's SC/ST list

A Scheduled Caste certificate from one State does not by itself give reservation benefits under another State's scheme

Maharashtra's Maratha quota was struck down — there were no extraordinary circumstances to cross the 50% limit. The 102nd Amendment was upheld (not struck down), but it was read as giving the power to identify SEBCs only to the Centre.

Persons with disabilities are entitled to reservation in promotion

A 7-judge bench (6:1 majority) held that States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, based on empirical data; overruled the E.V. Chinnaiah case

head: Point
Fact

124th Constitution Amendment Bill (Lok Sabha, Jan 2019)
Inserted

blocks.title: Central EWS criteria (OM 31 Jan 2019)
head: Test
Rule
rows: Income

Family gross annual income must be below ₹8 lakh, counting all sources (salary, agriculture, business, profession), for the financial year before the year of application. Example: salary ₹6.8 lakh + farm income ₹1.4 lakh = ₹8.2 lakh, so NOT eligible.
Excluded if family owns ANY of

5 acres or more of agricultural land; a residential flat of 1,000 sq ft or more; a residential plot of 100 sq yd or more in notified municipalities; or a residential plot of 200 sq yd or more in other areas. (Owning a car is NOT a test.)
Clubbing
Property held in different places is added together (clubbed) to apply these limits
Family
'Family' means the applicant, parents, brothers and sisters below 18, spouse, and children below 18
Backlog
An unfilled EWS vacancy is NOT carried forward to the next year (this is a rule in the OM, not a bar in the Constitution)
Exempt posts
Certain scientific and technical research posts above the lowest Group A grade are exempt from EWS reservation

items: Art 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Enforcing any disability (restriction) arising from untouchability is an offence punishable by law.

'Untouchability' is not defined in the Constitution or in the PCR (Protection of Civil Rights) Act. The Mysore High Court held that it means the historical caste-based practice (for example, stopping someone from using a public well because they are seen as 'polluting'), not a social boycott of a few individuals. The lack of a definition does not make Art 17 unenforceable.
Art 17 binds private individuals too, and the State must act to stop such violations — PUDR case (1982).
Art 17 and Art 23(1) themselves declare these acts to be offences; Parliament makes the law fixing the punishment under Art 35(a)(ii) — see the Art 33–35 card.

blocks.title: Laws under Art 17
head: Law
Fact
rows: Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955
Amended in 1976 and renamed the Protection of Civil Rights (PCR) Act — still cited as the 1955 Act
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989
Enacted because the PCR Act proved inadequate; it gives effect to Art 14, Art 15 and Art 17. Its Preamble mentions Special Courts for trial, and relief and rehabilitation of victims.
Atrocities (examples)
Examples: dumping waste or animal carcasses near an SC/ST person's premises; insulting them by caste name in public view; forcing them to leave their house or village
Punishments

Giving false evidence that gets an SC/ST person convicted of a capital offence (one punishable by death): life imprisonment and fine; if the innocent person is executed as a result: death penalty. Most offences under Section 3(1): 6 months to 5 years' imprisonment and fine.
Investigation
Investigation by an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP)
Subhash Kashinath Mahajan case (2018)
Criticised for diluting the Act — it allowed anticipatory bail (bail before arrest) and required a preliminary inquiry before registering a case
2018 amendment
Parliament inserted Section 18A to restore the strict provisions (no preliminary inquiry, no anticipatory bail); upheld in the Prathvi Raj Chauhan case (2020)

sections.heading: Art 18 — Abolition of titles and national awards

blocks.title: Four provisions of Art 18
head: Clause
Rule
rows: The State shall not give any title to anyone (citizen OR foreigner), except military or academic distinctions
A citizen of India cannot accept any title from a foreign State — this ban is absolute; even the President's consent cannot allow it
A foreigner holding an office of profit or trust under the State needs the President's consent to accept a title from any foreign State
A citizen or foreigner holding such an office needs the President's consent to accept any gift (present), payment (emolument) or office from a foreign State
blocks.note: Art 18 ends hereditary colonial titles such as Maharaja, Rai Bahadur and Dewan Bahadur.

blocks.title: National awards
items: Balaji Raghavan case (1995): Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri are NOT titles under Art 18. But they must not be used before or after a person's name (as prefix or suffix); if misused, the award can be forfeited (taken back).
The awards were instituted in 1954; discontinued in 1977 by the Janata government of Morarji Desai; revived in 1980 by Indira Gandhi.
Padma awards were interrupted twice (not once): in 1978–79 and in 1993–97.
At most 3 Bharat Ratnas can be given in a year (not 5). Padma awards: at most 120 a year, not counting posthumous awards and awards to foreigners.
Bharat Ratna 2024 was given to 5 persons: Karpoori Thakur, L.K. Advani, P.V. Narasimha Rao, Chaudhary Charan Singh and M.S. Swaminathan.
In the Table of Precedence (official order of rank at ceremonies), Bharat Ratna holders are at entry 7A — this is ceremonial only and gives no authority over ministers.
Art 14 is for all persons, including foreigners and companies; Art 15 and Art 16 are for citizens only.
Art 16(2) includes 'descent' and 'residence' as banned grounds; Art 15(1) does not.
Residence rules for jobs: under Art 16(3), Parliament does it by law; under Art 371D (AP and Telangana), the President does it by order.

Which Amendment added what: Art 15(4) — 1st Amendment (1951, after Champakam case); Art 15(5) — 93rd (2005, after Inamdar case); Art 16(4A) — 77th; Art 16(4B) — 81st; Art 335 proviso — 82nd; consequential seniority — 85th; Art 15(6) and Art 16(6) — 103rd.
Art 15(2), Art 17 (and also Art 23 and Art 24) can be enforced against private persons.
EWS: income limit ₹8 lakh, including agricultural income; unfilled vacancies are not carried forward; upheld 3:2 in the Janhit Abhiyan case.
The 105th Amendment (2021) restored the States' power to make their own SEBC lists after the Maratha case; the 102nd Amendment was NOT struck down.
Bharat Ratna: at most 3 a year; national awards are not titles. Art 14, Art 19 and Art 21 together form the 'golden triangle' (Maneka Gandhi case, 1978).

subcards.title: Right to Freedom (Art 19–22)
subcards.summary: Article 19 gives six freedoms; Article 20 protects people accused of crimes; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; Article 21A gives the right to education; Article 22 gives safeguards against arrest and detention.
at_a_glance: Articles 19 to 22, under the heading 'Right to Freedom' in Part III
Six freedoms, for citizens only. Originally there were seven – the seventh, right to property [19(1)(f)], was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978).

Three protections for all persons: no ex post facto law (no punishment for an act that was legal when done), no double jeopardy (no prosecution and punishment twice for the same offence), no self-incrimination (no forcing an accused to give evidence against himself). Cannot be suspended even in an Emergency (Art 359).

Life and personal liberty, for all persons. The words 'procedure established by law' were read by the Supreme Court in the Maneka Gandhi case (1978) to mean a procedure that is 'fair, just and reasonable'.
Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years – added by the 86th Amendment (2002); came into force, together with the RTE (Right to Education) Act, on 1 April 2010.
Safeguards for a person under ordinary arrest (clauses 1 and 2) and safeguards for a person under preventive detention, that is, detention without trial (clauses 4 to 7)

Art 14, Art 19 and Art 21 work together: a law that limits life or liberty must be fair (14), reasonable (19) and follow a just procedure (21). This 'golden triangle' rule was set by the Maneka Gandhi case (1978).

sections.heading: Art 19: six freedoms and the grounds on which they can be restricted

blocks.title: Article 19(1) freedoms and their restriction clauses
head: Clause
Freedom
Restriction clause
Grounds (only these)
rows: Speech and expression

Sovereignty and integrity of India (added by 16th Amendment, 1963); security of the State; friendly relations with foreign States (added by 1st Amendment, 1951); public order (added by 1st Amendment); decency or morality; contempt of court; defamation; incitement to an offence (added by 1st Amendment)
Assemble peaceably and without arms
Sovereignty and integrity of India (added by 16th Amendment); public order
Form associations or unions or co-operative societies (the words 'co-operative societies' were added by the 97th Amendment, 2011)
Sovereignty and integrity of India (added by 16th Amendment); public order; morality
Move freely throughout the territory of India
Interests of the general public; protection of interests of any Scheduled Tribe
Reside and settle in any part of India
Same grounds as 19(1)(d): interests of the general public; protection of interests of any Scheduled Tribe
Acquire, hold and dispose of property
Removed by the 44th Amendment (1978). Property is now only a legal (constitutional) right under Art 300A, not a Fundamental Right.
Practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business

Interests of the general public; the State may fix professional or technical qualifications needed for a job [19(6)(i)]; the State, or a corporation owned or controlled by the State, may run any trade, business, industry or service, keeping citizens fully or partly out of it (State monopoly) [19(6)(ii), added by 1st Amendment]
blocks.note: These are NOT grounds under 19(2): sedition, 'general public interest', public health. 'Public order' is common to 19(2), 19(3) and 19(4). 'Morality' appears in 19(2) (along with decency) and in 19(4), but NOT in 19(3). 'General public interest' appears only in 19(5) and 19(6).

blocks.title: Key features
items: Art 19 is available only to citizens – not to foreigners, and not to companies as such. But shareholders who are citizens can still claim it (Bennett Coleman case, 1972).
Freedoms are not absolute: the State may impose 'reasonable' restrictions, and courts decide whether a restriction is reasonable.

Restrictions can be imposed only by a law, and only on the grounds listed in clauses (2) to (6). The power to limit Fundamental Rights lies with the legislature, not with the Supreme Court (the court only checks whether the restriction is reasonable).
Freedom of movement under Art 19 covers movement only inside India. The right to travel abroad and to return to India comes under Art 21 (Maneka Gandhi case, 1978).

Freedom of expression is not limited to India's territory, but expression abroad is still subject to the restrictions in Art 19(2) (Justice Chandrachud in the Maneka Gandhi case). Freedom of movement under Art 19(1)(d) does NOT cover foreign countries.
A prisoner or detenu (a person held under preventive detention) loses freedom of movement, but keeps freedom of speech and expression and other rights that fit with being detained.

Movement of prostitutes may be restricted (on grounds of public health and public morals). The Bombay High Court upheld restrictions on the movement of persons with AIDS. Tribal areas can be closed to outsiders [19(5)].
Assembly: only on public land, and only peaceful and unarmed. It includes meetings, demonstrations and processions. It does not include a right to strike.

Association: includes forming political parties, companies, unions and clubs; the right to continue the association; and the negative right not to join any association. Getting official recognition for an association is not a Fundamental Right. There is no Fundamental Right to strike, to effective bargaining or to declare a lock-out.

Profession: there is no right to carry on immoral or dangerous trades (such as trafficking, harmful drugs, explosives) – these can be totally banned or allowed only with a licence. When the State runs a monopoly under 19(6)(ii), it need not prove that the monopoly is reasonable.

Speech of legislators inside the House: Art 105(1) (Parliament) and Art 194(1) (State Legislature) give freedom of speech, subject to the Constitution and the rules and standing orders of the House. Art 105(2) and Art 194(2) give immunity from court cases for anything said or any vote given in the House or its committees.

blocks.title: Assembly restrictions in criminal law
head: Provision
Content
rows: Sec 144 of CrPC 1973 (now replaced by Sec 163 of BNSS 2023)
An Executive Magistrate can pass an order in urgent cases of nuisance or feared danger; such an order can stop an assembly, meeting or procession
Sec 141 IPC (unlawful assembly)

An assembly of 5 or more persons with a common unlawful object – for example, to resist the law, to occupy property by force, to commit mischief or trespass, to force someone to do an illegal act, or to overawe (frighten) the government

blocks.title: Amendments touching Art 19–22 (chronological)
head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Added 'public order', 'friendly relations with foreign States' and 'incitement to an offence' to 19(2); added 19(6)(ii) (State monopoly in trade); also inserted Art 15(4). Passed by the Provisional Parliament (before the first Lok Sabha was elected).
Added 'sovereignty and integrity of India' to 19(2), (3), (4)

Removed 19(1)(f) and Art 31 (property); inserted Art 300A; reduced the period after which an Advisory Board must review preventive detention in Art 22(4) from 3 months to 2 months – but this clause has NOT yet been brought into force; made Art 20 and Art 21 non-suspendable during an Emergency
Inserted Art 21A; replaced Art 45 with a new one (early childhood care up to 6 years); added Art 51A(k). (It was introduced in Parliament as the 93rd Amendment Bill.)
Added 'co-operative societies' to 19(1)(c); inserted Art 43B (a DPSP – Directive Principle) and Part IXB (Art 243ZH to 243ZT). Act passed in 2011, in force from 15 Feb 2012.

blocks.title: 97th Amendment – Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)
items: The Gujarat High Court (2013) and the Supreme Court (2021, by 2:1 majority) struck down Part IXB in so far as it dealt with State co-operative societies. Reasons: co-operative societies are a State List subject, and ratification by half the States under Art 368(2) was not obtained.
Part IXB still survives for multi-State co-operative societies. The change to 19(1)(c) and Art 43B were not struck down.

blocks.text: Citizens-only vs all-persons rights and the full amendment table → see Fundamental Rights: overview

sections.heading: Art 19 cases: speech, press, assembly, association and trade

blocks.title: Rights read into Art 19(1)(a) (Laxmikanth list)
items: Right to spread one's views (freedom of circulation); freedom of the press; freedom of commercial advertisements; right against telephone tapping; right to telecast (no government monopoly on electronic media); right against a bandh called by a political party or organisation
Right to know about government activities (right to information); freedom of silence; right against pre-censorship of a newspaper; right to demonstrate or picket – but NOT a right to strike

Right to fly the National Flag; voters' right to know the antecedents (background) of candidates; right to choose the medium of instruction at the primary stage; right to express one's gender identity; right to reply
Right to post information and videos on the internet and social media; film-makers' right to exhibit films; right to access information through the internet

Freedom of the press is NOT expressly written in the Constitution – the courts treat it as implied in 19(1)(a). The NCRWC (National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution, chaired by Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah, report 2002) recommended adding it expressly.

blocks.title: Speech and press
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)
A ban on the entry of a journal into the State was struck down; freedom of speech includes freedom to circulate (distribute) it
This case led to 'public order' being added as a ground in 19(2) by the 1st Amendment
Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950)
An order to scrutinise a newspaper before publication (pre-censorship) was quashed under Art 19(2) as it stood at that time
Against pre-censorship
Sakal Papers v. Union of India (1962)
Fixing a newspaper's price according to its number of pages violates freedom of the press
Struck down the price-page schedule
Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962)
Upheld the sedition offence (Sec 124A of IPC) but read it down (narrowed it) to cover only acts that tend to cause public disorder or incite violence
Sedition is NOT a ground in 19(2)
Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar (1962)
A blanket ban on all demonstrations by government servants was struck down; peaceful demonstration is protected by 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b); but there is no right to strike
Demonstration is allowed; strike is not a right
K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970)
Prior censorship of films (checking before release) is valid if it stays within constitutional limits and has procedural safeguards
Films are treated differently from the press (films can be pre-censored)
Bennett Coleman v. Union of India (1972)
A newsprint policy limiting newspapers to 10 pages violated 19(1)(a) and Art 14; shareholders who are citizens can claim their rights through the company
Press freedom covers both quantity (pages) and circulation
State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975)
People have a right to know every public act done by public officials (Justice Mathew); this right is not absolute – genuine security concerns can limit it
Starting point of the right to information
S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989)
A film cleared by the censor board cannot be stopped just because some group threatens violence; the State must protect the expression
No 'heckler's veto' – a threatening crowd cannot decide what others may say
Tata Press v. MTNL (1995)
Commercial speech (advertisements) is protected by 19(1)(a), subject to the restrictions in 19(2)
Advertisements are protected speech
Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)
Airwaves are public property; there is a right to telecast, but no unlimited right to use any frequency; airwaves must be regulated by a public authority
Right to telecast; no government monopoly
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)

Children of the Jehovah's Witness faith who stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem could not be expelled from school – protected by Art 19(1)(a) (freedom of silence) and Art 25 (religion); no law forces anyone to sing
Freedom of silence
PUCL v. Union of India (18 Dec 1996)

Telephone tapping affects privacy (Art 21) and expression (Art 19(1)(a)). Under Sec 5(2) of the Telegraph Act, tapping is allowed only in a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, and the reasons must be recorded in writing
Telephone-tapping safeguards
Union of India v. ADR (2002); PUCL v. Union of India (2003)
Voters have a right to know candidates' criminal record, assets and education – this is part of 19(1)(a)
Led to candidates filing affidavits from 2003 (including assets of spouse and dependants)
Union of India v. Naveen Jindal (2004)
Flying the National Flag with respect and dignity is part of 19(1)(a); it is subject to reasonable restrictions
Led to the Flag Code being relaxed so citizens can fly the flag
S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010)

Quashed the criminal complaints against the actress for her remarks on pre-marital sex and live-in relationships; an opinion that is unpopular or morally disapproved is not a crime – courts must check whether the exact elements of the offence in the law are present
Something being immoral does not make it a crime
PUCL v. Union of India – NOTA case (2013)

The right to vote is a statutory right (given by law, not a Fundamental Right), but casting a vote is a form of expression under 19(1)(a); secrecy must protect a voter who rejects all candidates – so NOTA ('None of the Above') was introduced
NOTA has no electoral effect – the highest-polling candidate wins even if NOTA gets more votes
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
Sec 66A of the IT Act struck down – its words ('annoying', 'inconvenient') were vague and too wide, and it had a chilling effect (people stop speaking out of fear)
Protects online speech
Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016)
Criminal defamation (Sec 499 and 500 of IPC) upheld as a reasonable restriction; a person's reputation is part of Art 21
Defamation is one of the grounds in 19(2)
Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India
An interim order in Nov 2016 made playing the National Anthem compulsory before films; the order of 9 Jan 2018 made it optional (directory, not mandatory)
National Anthem in cinemas
Faheema Shirin R.K. v. State of Kerala (2019, Kerala High Court)
A hostel ban on using mobile phones was struck down; internet access is part of the right to education and the right to privacy under Art 21 (the hostel can still make rules for discipline)
First ruling on 'internet access' as a right (by a High Court, not the Supreme Court)
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)

Freedom of speech and freedom of trade carried on over the internet are protected by 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); any restriction must be proportionate (no more than needed); suspending the internet indefinitely is not allowed
Did NOT declare internet access itself to be a Fundamental Right
Prashant Bhushan contempt case (sentence given 31 Aug 2020)
Fine of ₹1. If not paid: 3 months' simple imprisonment and a 3-year ban from practising law – these applied only if the fine was not paid
Contempt of court is one of the grounds in 19(2)
Vinod Dua v. Union of India (2021)

Quashed the sedition FIR filed in Himachal Pradesh against the journalist (applying the limits set in Kedar Nath); but refused his request that a committee must clear any FIR against journalists with 10 or more years of experience
Criticism of the government by the press is not sedition
Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (3 Jan 2023)

No restrictions beyond those in 19(2) can be placed on a minister's speech; rights under Art 19 and Art 21 can be enforced even against private persons, not just the State (called 'horizontal' application)
Decided by a 4:1 majority
ADR v. Union of India – Electoral Bonds case (15 Feb 2024)
The Electoral Bond Scheme was struck down, mainly because it violated voters' right to information under 19(1)(a)
Transparency in political party funding

blocks.title: Sedition after the new criminal laws
head: Point
Position
rows: Sec 124A of IPC (sedition)
Put on hold (kept in abeyance) by a Supreme Court order (S.G. Vombatkere case, May 2022). The IPC was later replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, in force from 1 July 2024
Sec 152 of BNS
Does not use the word 'sedition'; it punishes acts that endanger the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
Explanation to Sec 152
Comments that disapprove of government measures and seek to change them by lawful means are not an offence, as long as they do not excite the activities that the section prohibits

blocks.title: Assembly, association and trade
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Damyanti Naranga v. Union of India (1971)
The right of association includes the right to continue the association with the members it chose voluntarily; a law that forces outsiders into it violates 19(1)(c)
Protects who the members of an association are
Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India (1981)
19(1)(g) gives no right to continue in a particular job or post; remedies under industrial (labour) law are still available
Also a PIL case on locus standi (who has the right to approach the court)
CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar (1997)
The Kerala High Court (1997) first held that forced bandhs are unconstitutional; the Supreme Court agreed – a bandh violates the Fundamental Rights of other citizens
A bandh (forced shutdown) is different from a hartal (voluntary strike), which is not banned
T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003)
Government employees have no fundamental, legal, moral or equitable right to strike
Strike is not part of 19(1)(c)
Haryana State Employment of Local Candidates Act, 2020
The law gave 75% of private-sector jobs to local residents; it was struck down by the Punjab and Haryana High Court (17 Nov 2023)
Held to violate Art 14 and 19(1)(g)

blocks.title: Right to Information Act, 2005
head: Point
Fact
rows: Constitutional basis
Implied in Art 19(1)(a) (and Art 21) – so the right to information is both a Fundamental Right and a statutory (legal) right
Dates
Enacted 15 June 2005; some provisions came into force at once; the rest from the 120th day, that is, 12 Oct 2005

blocks.text: Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri case (a single company can be treated as a class by itself) → see Right to Equality

sections.heading: Art 20: protection in respect of conviction for offences

blocks.title: Article 20 – available to all persons (citizen, foreigner, company)
head: Clause
Protection
Limits
rows: No ex post facto (retrospective) criminal law: no one can be convicted except for breaking a law that was in force when the act was done; and no one can get a penalty greater than the one in force at that time

Applies only to criminal laws – civil and tax laws can be made retrospective (they are tested under other Articles). It bars only conviction and sentence, not trial: a later change in trial procedure or in the court is valid. It does not stop a lighter penalty made later from being given to the accused – that depends on the statute (its repeal and savings clause). It cannot be claimed against preventive detention or a demand for security (bond).

No double jeopardy – no one can be prosecuted AND punished for the same offence more than once (Latin maxims: autrefois convict – 'already convicted'; nemo debet bis vexari – 'no one should be troubled twice')

Applies only to proceedings before a court or judicial tribunal – a departmental inquiry and dismissal from service do not bar a criminal prosecution. It needs an earlier prosecution plus punishment – so by itself it does not bar a retrial after acquittal (narrower than the US rule). 'Same offence' is decided by comparing the legal elements of the two offences, not just common facts.
No person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself (bar on testimonial compulsion)

Covers oral and documentary evidence. Does not cover being forced to give material objects, thumb impression, specimen signature or handwriting, blood samples, or showing the body. Applies only to criminal proceedings.

blocks.title: Cases on Art 20(3)
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961)
Fingerprints and specimen handwriting or signature are physical material used for identification, not 'testimony' – so taking them does not violate 20(3)
Physical evidence is allowed; testimonial (personal-knowledge) evidence cannot be forced
Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978)
20(3) applies during police questioning too, not only in court; heavy psychological pressure can amount to compulsion
Right to stay silent during police questioning
Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010)

Forcing a person to undergo narcoanalysis, polygraph (lie-detector) or BEAP (brain-mapping) tests violates Art 20(3) and Art 21, because the results are testimonial. These tests are allowed only with consent and safeguards, and even then the results cannot be used as evidence by themselves – only facts discovered later because of them can be used (under Sec 27 of the Evidence Act)
Public interest cannot weaken the protection of 20(3)

blocks.title: Terms
items: Ex post facto law means a retrospective law (one that applies to acts done before it was made). Every ex post facto law is retrospective.
Under Art 359 (as amended by the 44th Amendment), the enforcement of Art 20 and Art 21 can never be suspended, even during an Emergency.
Art 20 comes under the heading 'Right to Freedom' – so 'double jeopardy' belongs to the Right to Freedom category (not Right to Equality).

sections.heading: Art 21: from the Gopalan case to the Maneka case (procedure established by law vs due process)

blocks.text: Art 21: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' It is available to citizens and non-citizens. It protects against arbitrary action by the executive AND (after the Maneka Gandhi case) by the legislature.

blocks.title: A.K. Gopalan case (1950) vs Maneka Gandhi case (1978)
head: Aspect
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
rows: Facts
A communist leader (A.K. Gopalan) was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950
Her existing passport was impounded (taken away) under Sec 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967
Reading of Art 21
Narrow: Art 21 protects only against executive action; any law made by a competent legislature is enough, whatever its procedure
Wide: the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable – not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive – and must follow natural justice (fair hearing, no bias)
Personal liberty
Means only freedom of the body (from physical restraint)
Given the widest meaning; covers many rights (such as travel abroad)
Articles 14, 19, 21
Each Article is separate and independent ('watertight compartments') – a law is tested under one Article only
The Articles are linked, not separate – a law under Art 21 must also pass the tests of Art 14 and Art 19 (this link is called the 'golden triangle')
Due process
Rejected the US idea of 'due process of law' (where courts also judge whether the law itself is fair); the majority refused to read it into Art 21
In effect brought in substantive 'due process' (courts can test the fairness of the law itself), even though the words of Art 21 were not changed
Other holdings
Sec 14 of the Preventive Detention Act 1950 (which barred telling the court the grounds of detention) was held void but severable – it was cut out and the rest of the Act was upheld
A hearing after the decision (post-decisional hearing) was acceptable on the facts of the case; 'life' means life with human dignity

blocks.title: Procedure established by law vs due process of law
head: Aspect
Procedure established by law (India, from Japan)
Due process of law (USA, 5th and 14th Amendments)
rows: Court checks
Only whether a valid law exists and whether its procedure was followed
Also whether the law and procedure are fair and reasonable
Judicial review
Narrower scope for the court
Wider scope for the court
Essence
Legislative supremacy (the legislature has the final word)
Natural justice – fairness (the court can judge the law itself)

blocks.title: Constituent Assembly and natural justice
items: Ambedkar on 'due process': he said it is about the relation between the legislature and the judiciary, and about adjusting a federal arrangement. So the Constituent Assembly chose 'procedure established by law' (the Japanese model).
Two rules of natural justice: audi alteram partem means 'hear the other side' (fair hearing); nemo judex in causa sua means 'no one should be a judge in his own case' (rule against bias).

A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India (1969): the rule against bias was applied because a candidate himself sat on the selection board; natural justice applies to administrative action too. Art 14 does not expressly list the rules of natural justice.
Habeas corpus (a writ ordering that a detained person be produced before the court) secures personal liberty – see Right to Constitutional Remedies.

blocks.text: Habeas corpus and other writs → see Right to Constitutional Remedies

sections.heading: Art 21 expanded: rights read into it and landmark cases

blocks.title: Rights declared part of Art 21 (Laxmikanth list of 39)
items: Right to human dignity; decent environment (pollution-free water and air, protection from hazardous industries); livelihood; privacy; shelter; health; free education up to 14 years; free legal aid

Right against solitary confinement; to a speedy trial; against handcuffing; against inhuman treatment; against delay in execution of a death sentence; to travel abroad; against bonded labour; against harassment in custody

Right to emergency medical aid (a doctor's help); timely treatment in a government hospital; not to be driven out of a State; fair trial; a prisoner's necessities of life; women's decency and dignity; against public hanging

Right to a road in hilly areas; information; reputation; appeal against conviction; family pension; social and economic justice; against bar fetters (iron chains on prisoners); an appropriate life-insurance policy; sleep

Right to freedom from noise pollution; sustainable development; opportunity; decent burial or cremation; to marry a person of one's choice; to die with dignity (passive euthanasia – withdrawing life support); against the adverse effects of climate change

NOT recognised as part of Art 21: right to die or commit suicide; active euthanasia (giving a lethal drug); right to work (this is only a Directive Principle, Art 41); right to strike; internet access itself (the Supreme Court has not declared it a Fundamental Right).

blocks.title: Life, dignity, health and livelihood
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967)
Right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty
Confirmed again in the Maneka Gandhi case
Francis Coralie Mullin (1981)

Ordered release of bonded labourers – Art 21 read together with Art 39(e), 39(f), 41 and 42
Dignity of labour

Basis of the Good Samaritan law (protection for people who help accident victims)

Shelter

Denying timely emergency treatment in a government hospital violates Art 21; the Court ordered compensation and gave directions to improve services; lack of money is no excuse
Health

Led to the National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013 (Bill introduced in 2011)
Ashray Adhikar Abhiyan v. Union of India (2002)
Decent burial or cremation of unclaimed bodies of homeless persons – dignity continues even after death
Dignity of the dead

Pollution

Environmental education

Sustainable development

Public trust doctrine

Noise

Compensation

Delayed execution

Bail
Hussainara (1979); S.P. Gupta (1981)

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters

Right to life does not include a right to die; Sec 309 of IPC (attempt to suicide) is valid
Early High Court view

Sec 309 of IPC struck down – the right to die was held to be included in Art 21
Later overruled by Gian Kaur (1996)
Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996)
Art 21 does NOT include a right to die; Sec 309 is valid (this overruled the Rathinam case)
Current law on suicide
Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011)

Passive euthanasia guidelines

Living will (procedure made simpler in 2023)

First actual passive euthanasia (as of Nov 2026)

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters

Both held that privacy is not a Fundamental Right
Overruled on this point in 2017 (Puttaswamy)

Privacy versus publishing a prisoner's autobiography – the press may publish matters that are in public records
Balancing privacy and press freedom
Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)

These guidelines applied until the POSH Act, 2013 was made
Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)
Registration of marriages made compulsory for all religions
Marriage

Sec 377 of IPC read down (narrowed) so it did not cover consensual acts between adults in private; did not reopen cases already closed
Step 1 of the Sec 377 story
Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation (2013)
Supreme Court reversed the Naz judgment – Sec 377 held valid
Step 2; later referred to a Constitution Bench for reconsideration (2018)
NALSA v. Union of India (2014)

Transgender persons are the 'third gender'; they have a right to their self-identified gender without surgery; expressing gender identity is part of 19(1)(a); they must be treated as socially and educationally backward classes for admissions AND public appointments
Gender identity

A 9-judge Bench (Chief Justice J.S. Khehar) held privacy is a basic part of Art 21 and of the freedoms in Part III. It overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh on this point, and also the ADM Jabalpur case (1976). Any restriction on privacy must meet three tests: legality (a law), need (a legitimate aim) and proportionality

Puttaswamy (Aadhaar case), 26 Sep 2018
A separate 5-judge Bench upheld the Aadhaar Act, but struck down some of its provisions
Different from the 2017 privacy case
Shafin Jahan v. Asokan (Hadiya case, 2018); Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018)

Marriage choice

Adult's choice of partner

Sec 377 held unconstitutional in so far as it made consensual acts between adults a crime; the Koushal judgment was overruled
Step 3 of the Sec 377 story (final)

A DNA test cannot be ordered as a routine matter in a property case; the court must balance privacy against the need for it, especially when other evidence is available
Privacy

Same-sex marriage

Upheld Sec 5(v) of the Hindu Marriage Act, which bars sapinda marriages (marriage between close blood relatives)
Choice of partner has limits

blocks.title: The three education provisions of the 86th Amendment
head: Article
Category
Content

The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14, in the manner the State decides by law (elementary education only, not higher education)
45 (substituted)
DPSP (Directive Principle)
Early childhood care and education for all children until they complete 6 years

Related: Art 24

head: Provision
Fact

Classes I to VIII

Samacheer Kalvi (Tamil Nadu's uniform school syllabus)

blocks.title: Two parts of Art 22
head: Aspect
Ordinary arrest – clauses (1) and (2)
Preventive detention – clauses (4) to (7)
rows: Nature
Punitive – the person is arrested for a criminal or quasi-criminal act already done
Detention without trial – precautionary, based on suspicion, to prevent a future act
Rights

(1) To be told the grounds of arrest 'as soon as may be'; (2) to consult and be defended by a lawyer of one's choice – from the time of arrest, not only after the charge-sheet; (3) to be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, not counting travel time; (4) to be released after 24 hours unless the magistrate allows further custody

Detention cannot exceed 3 months unless an Advisory Board reports there is sufficient cause; the grounds must be told to the detenu as soon as may be (but facts against the public interest need not be disclosed – clause 6); the detenu must get the earliest chance to make a representation against the order (clause 5)
Not available to

Not available to enemy aliens, or to persons arrested under a preventive detention law [clause (3)]. Also does not apply to arrest on a court's order, civil arrest, arrest for not paying tax, or deportation of aliens
Who
Citizens and aliens (except enemy aliens)
Citizens and aliens
Lawyer
Yes – right to a lawyer of one's choice
No – the right to a lawyer given in clauses (1) and (2) does not apply to a preventive detenu

blocks.title: Preventive detention details
items: Advisory Board: made up of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be High Court judges [22(4)(a)]; it must report before the 3 months are over.

Art 22(7): Parliament may lay down by law (a) the circumstances and classes of cases in which a person can be detained for more than 3 months without the Advisory Board's opinion; (b) the maximum period of detention; (c) the procedure of the Advisory Board.

The 44th Amendment (1978) reduced the 3-month period to 2 months and changed how the Advisory Board is formed – but this part has NOT been brought into force, so 3 months still applies. A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982): the court cannot force the Government to bring it into force; the National Security Act was upheld.

Who can make preventive detention laws: only Parliament – for defence, foreign affairs and security of India (Union List, Entry 9); both Parliament and States – for security of a State, public order, and supplies and services essential to the community (Concurrent List, Entry 3).

No other democratic country makes preventive detention part of its Constitution; it is unknown in the USA; Britain used it only during the World Wars. In colonial India: Bengal State Prisoners Regulation 1818, Defence of India Act 1939.
The NCRWC (National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution, 2002) recommended a maximum detention period of 6 months.
Keeping a person in police custody beyond 24 hours without a magistrate's order is possible only under preventive detention (and for enemy aliens).
Art 355: the Union has a duty to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance (see the Emergency topic).

Held

On request, a friend or relative must be told about the arrest and the place of detention; the arrested person must be told of this right; an entry must be made in the police diary; the magistrate must check that these rules were followed
Right to have someone informed of the arrest
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
Laid down detailed arrest guidelines – arrest memo, medical examination, police officers must wear clear identification, etc. The case began as a letter from a legal aid body, treated as a PIL
Against violence in police custody
Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014)
No automatic arrest for offences punishable with up to 7 years in jail; police must record reasons for arresting
Arrest only after going through a checklist

Grounds of arrest in writing

Failing to tell the arrested person the grounds of arrest violates Art 22(1) – the arrest becomes illegal
As of Nov 2026

blocks.text: Art 358 vs Art 359 and suspension of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency → see Art 33–35 and suspension of FRs

items: Art 19 = 6 freedoms, for citizens only. Art 20, 21 and 22 = for all persons (but Art 22(1) and 22(2) are not for enemy aliens). So a foreigner cannot claim 19(1)(g) (right to trade), but can claim Art 14 and Art 21.
Sedition, 'public interest' (for speech) and 'public health' are NOT grounds in 19(2). Morality is not a ground in 19(3) (assembly).
Freedom of the press, right to information, right to know candidates' antecedents (background), and voting for NOTA are all implied in 19(1)(a) – they are not written in its words.
The Maneka Gandhi case did NOT change the words of Art 21 – 'procedure established by law' still stands. The majority in the Gopalan case rejected 'due process'.

Art 20(2) bars only a second prosecution AND punishment for the same offence; it does not cover departmental action, or a retrial after acquittal. Art 20(1) applies only to criminal laws; trial procedure can still be changed later.
Handwriting, fingerprints and blood samples are not testimonial evidence (can be taken by force). Forced narcoanalysis, polygraph or BEAP (brain-mapping) tests violate 20(3) (Selvi case, 2010).

86th Amendment 2002 (introduced as the 93rd Amendment Bill) → added Art 21A, new Art 45 and Art 51A(k); in force from 1 April 2010. Education was moved to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment 1976 – NOT by the 76th or 86th.

Preventive detention: maximum 3 months without Advisory Board (the 44th Amendment's 2 months is not in force); the right to a lawyer and the 24-hour rule do NOT apply to it. Separately: internet access itself is not a Fundamental Right (only the Kerala High Court said so, in Faheema Shirin).

All persons — both citizens and foreigners
Both the State AND private persons (for example, a private employer)
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956; Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976
Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 — renamed in 2016 as the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986
People's Union for Democratic Rights (PUDR) (1982), Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984), M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996)

Provision
Nature
