sections.heading: Article 23: traffic in human beings and forced labour

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Traffic in human beings

Includes: (a) selling and buying men, women and children like goods; (b) immoral traffic in women and children, including prostitution; (c) the devadasi system (girls dedicated to temples and sexually exploited); (d) slavery
Begar
Compulsory work WITHOUT any payment. It was an old Indian system in which zamindars (landlords) forced tenants to work for them free
Forced labour
Making a person work against his or her will. The 'similar forms' of forced labour in Art 23 include bonded labour (working to repay a debt, without freedom to leave)
'Force'

'Force' includes physical force, legal force AND the pressure of economic circumstances — for example, a poor person forced to work for less than the minimum wage. The worker need not be physically held back

blocks.title: Laws made under Art 23
head: Law (year)
Purpose
rows: Minimum Wages Act, 1948
Fixes minimum wages. Paying below the minimum wage counts as forced labour

Punishes trafficking and prostitution. Its original name was 'Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act'. A 1986 amendment renamed it, but the year in its title stays 1956 — it is not a new 1986 Act
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970
Regulates contract labour
Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976
Abolishes bonded labour. The legal DEFINITION of 'bonded labour system' is given in this Act, not in the Constitution
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
Equal pay for men and women for the same work
blocks.note: The Right to Education (RTE) Act 2009 is NOT a law under Art 23 — it implements Art 21A (right to education).

blocks.title: Art 23(2) — compulsory public service
items: The State may make people do compulsory service for public purposes (such as military or social service), even without pay
But while imposing such service, the State may NOT discriminate on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class
Bans employing children below 14 years in any factory or mine. There is no need to prove that the factory or mine is hazardous — every factory and mine is covered
Also bans employing them in 'other hazardous employment' (for example, construction work and railways)

Art 24 itself does not ban harmless or innocent work. But work not covered by Art 24 is not automatically legal — ordinary laws (for example, the 1986 Child Labour Act as amended in 2016) may still ban it
Applies to private factory owners too, not only to the State
Example: employing a 12-year-old in a carpet factory violates Art 24

subcards.title: Freedom of Religion (Art 25–28)
subcards.summary: Freedom to follow, practise and spread religion — and the limits on it.
at_a_glance: Articles 25 to 28, in Part III (Fundamental Rights)
Freedom of conscience, and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion — a right of each individual
Rights of religious denominations (religious groups) — a collective right of the group
No tax to promote a particular religion
No religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions
Public order, morality and health apply to all; Art 25 is also subject to the other Fundamental Rights
Indian secularism is positive (the State gives equal respect to all religions); it is a basic feature of the Constitution — S.R. Bommai case (1994)

blocks.title: Not unlimited
items: The right to religion is NOT absolute — it is subject to public order, morality and health
Under Art 25(2), the State CAN make laws to regulate secular (non-religious) activities linked to religion, and laws for social reform
Compare: Art 19 rights are for citizens only, but Art 14, Art 21 and Art 25 are for all persons

blocks.title: Art 25(1) — four elements
head: Term
Meaning
rows: Freedom of conscience
Inner freedom to shape one's relationship with God or other beings in any way one wishes
Profess
Declare one's religious beliefs and faith openly and freely
Practise
Perform worship, rituals and ceremonies, and show one's beliefs openly
Propagate

Spread one's beliefs to others or explain the tenets (main teachings) of one's religion. This is NOT a right to convert another person, because forcible conversion violates the other person's freedom of conscience

blocks.title: Limits and State powers
items: Art 25(1) is subject to public order, morality and health, AND to the other provisions of Part III — so it does not automatically override other Fundamental Rights
Art 25(2)(a): the State may regulate or restrict economic, financial, political or other secular (non-religious) activity connected with religious practice — for example, temple finances
Art 25(2)(b): the State may make laws for social welfare and reform, or open public Hindu religious institutions (such as public temples) to all classes and sections of Hindus
Art 25 protects both beliefs (doctrines) and practices (rituals)

blocks.title: Two Explanations
head: Explanation
Content
rows: I
Wearing and carrying kirpans is included in the profession of the Sikh religion
II
In Art 25(2)(b), the word 'Hindus' includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists, and 'Hindu religious institutions' is read in the same way. This applies only to that sub-clause, not to the whole Constitution

blocks.title: Related clause (Art 16(5))
items: Art 16(5): a law may require a person holding an office in a religious or denominational institution (including a member of its governing body) to follow that religion or belong to that denomination
Art 16(5) does NOT allow general government jobs to be filled on the basis of religion

(b) manage its own affairs in matters of religion
(c) own and acquire movable and immovable property

blocks.title: What is a 'religious denomination' (S.P. Mittal case (1983))
items: Three tests: (1) a common faith (a system of beliefs that helps spiritual well-being), (2) a common organisation, and (3) a distinctive name
Ramakrishna Mission and Ananda Marga are religious denominations within Hinduism

Sri Aurobindo Society and Auroville are NOT a religious denomination, because the teachings of Sri Aurobindo were held to be a philosophy, not a religion. This was decided on the facts of that case; it is not a rule that every spiritual body is excluded

blocks.title: Art 27
items: No person can be forced to pay a tax whose money is specifically used to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination
This stops the State from favouring one religion; tax money may still be used for all religions equally

Art 27 bars a TAX, not a FEE. A fee is valid when charged for secular administration, for special services to pilgrims (such as safety and facilities), or for regulating endowments (religious trust property)

Religious instruction

blocks.title: What counts as religious instruction
items: Religious instruction means teaching a denomination's tenets (main teachings), rituals and forms of worship
Academic study of a saint's philosophy, or of religions in general, is NOT religious instruction

items: There is no official State religion, and the State does not discriminate on grounds of religion (Art 14, Art 15, Art 16)
All religious groups are equal before law. The devout (believer), the agnostic (one unsure whether God exists) and the atheist (non-believer) are all treated equally
The word 'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976); but Articles 25 to 28 already showed the secular intent before that
Secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution — S.R. Bommai case (1994)
Communal representation (separate seats reserved by religion) was abolished
Justice Gajendragadkar said: 'The State does not owe loyalty to any particular religion; it is not irreligious or anti-religious; it gives equal freedom to all religions'

Held

Whether something is an 'essential part' of a religion is decided mainly by that religion's own doctrines. Religious matters are protected, but secular and economic matters can be regulated by the State
Started the 'essential religious practices' test (only practices essential to a religion get protection)
Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977)

The right to propagate is not a right to convert another person. Madhya Pradesh and Orissa anti-conversion laws (against conversion by force, fraud or inducement) were held valid under Entry 1 of the State List (public order)
Anti-conversion laws upheld
S.P. Mittal v. Union of India (1983)
Laid down the three tests for a religious denomination; held that Aurobindo Society is not a denomination
Explained the meaning of 'denomination' in Art 26

Students of the Jehovah's Witness faith stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem; they could not be expelled. Expelling them violated Art 19(1)(a) (which includes the right to remain silent) and Art 25, and no law forces anyone to sing
Protects conscience; not singing is not the same as disrespect
Atheist Society of India v. Govt of AP (1992, Andhra Pradesh High Court)
The petition to ban religious rituals and symbols at State functions was dismissed; the State can still regulate religion on grounds of public order, morality and health
The atheists' challenge failed

A mosque is not an essential part of Islam, because namaz (prayer) can be offered anywhere; so the acquisition of Ayodhya land by the government was upheld
S.R. Bommai case (1994)
Secularism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution
Made secularism a basic feature
Manohar Joshi v. Nitin Bhaurao Patil (1995)
Using the word 'Hindutva' in an election speech is not by itself a corrupt practice; the context and manner of its use must be examined
Important for election law
A.S. Narayana Deekshitulu (1996)
Ending hereditary succession of archakas (temple priests) is regulation of a secular activity, so it is valid; but skill in the rituals is still required for appointment
Church of God (Full Gospel) (2000)
No religion requires prayers to be said through loudspeakers that disturb other people's peace
Supports noise limits on religious practice
Acharya Jagadishwarananda Avadhuta (2004)
Performing the Tandava dance in public processions is not an essential practice of the Ananda Margis, so it is not protected
Haji Ali case (2016, Bombay High Court)
On 26 Aug 2016, the ban on women entering the sanctum (inner shrine) was held to violate Art 14, Art 15 and Art 25; women's entry was restored on equal terms with men
Sabarimala case (2018) — Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala

On 28 Sep 2018, by a 4:1 majority, women of all ages were allowed to enter. The ban on women aged 10 to 50 violated Art 14, Art 21 and Art 25. Rule 3(b) of the 1965 Kerala rules was struck down. The Court said 'devotion cannot be subjected to gender discrimination'. Justice Indu Malhotra dissented (disagreed)
The first women to enter after the verdict were Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga (2 Jan 2019)

The right to propagate is not a right to convert; forcible conversion is not protected (Rev. Stainislaus, 1977)

subcards.title: Cultural & Educational Rights (Art 29–30)
subcards.summary: Article 29 protects the language, script and culture of any group of citizens; Article 30 lets religious and linguistic minorities set up and run their own educational institutions.
at_a_glance: Any section (group) of citizens — the majority community too, not only minorities
Only religious minorities and linguistic (language) minorities
No — the word 'minority' is not defined in the Constitution or in the National Commission for Minorities (NCM) Act 1992
Minority status is decided State by State, not on an all-India basis (TMA Pai case, 2002)
Kerala Education Bill (1958), St Xavier's (1974), TMA Pai (2002), Inamdar (2005)
Not absolute — the State can regulate; a minority has no right to maladminister (run the institution badly or unfairly)

sections.heading: Art 29: protection of interests of minorities

head: Clause
Provision
Right of
rows: Any section of citizens residing in India with a distinct language, script or culture of its own has the right to conserve it
A group (a section of citizens)
No citizen can be denied admission into an educational institution run by the State or receiving State aid (government funds) only because of religion, race, caste or language, or any of these
Each citizen as an individual, whatever community he belongs to

blocks.title: Key points
items: Article 29 protects citizens only. Contrast Art 25 (freedom of religion), which protects all persons, including foreigners.
It covers religious and linguistic minorities, but the Supreme Court held that it is not limited to minorities — 'section of citizens' includes the majority community too.
The group needs only one of the three — a distinct language, script or culture. For example, a distinct script alone is enough.

The right to conserve a language includes the right to agitate (campaign politically) for it. So election speeches demanding protection of a language are not a 'corrupt practice' (an illegal election act) under the Representation of the People Act (RPA) 1951.
Article 29(2) lists only four grounds: religion, race, caste and language. It does NOT list sex, place of birth, descent or residence — those appear in Art 15 and Art 16, so compare carefully.

Article 29(2) applies to institutions run by the State or receiving State aid — so a private institution that gets aid is covered. An institution that is only recognised (not aided) is not mentioned in the text.

blocks.text: See Right to Equality for Art 15(4), Art 15(5) and Art 15(6)

head: Clause
Provision
rows: All minorities, whether based on religion or language, have the right to establish (set up) and administer (manage) educational institutions of their choice

If the State compulsorily acquires (takes over by law) a minority institution's property, the compensation fixed must not restrict or abrogate (cancel) the right in clause 30(1). Added by the 44th Amendment, 1978 — the same amendment that deleted the Fundamental Right to property (Art 31)
When giving aid, the State shall not discriminate against an institution because it is managed by a minority (religious or linguistic)

blocks.title: Art 29 vs Art 30
head: Aspect
Art 29
Art 30
rows: Holders
Any section of citizens (majority or minority); under clause 29(2), any individual citizen
Only minorities — religious or linguistic
Content
Conserve language, script or culture; admission without discrimination
Establish and administer educational institutions
Minorities named

Religious and linguistic minorities only (not cultural or ethnic minorities)

children.label: Seek both recognition and aid: the State can regulate syllabus, standards, discipline and staff
Seek recognition only (no aid): the State can regulate the same matters as above
Seek neither recognition nor aid: free to run themselves, but must follow general laws (contract, labour, tax and others)

blocks.title: Scope (Malankara Syrian Catholic College case, 2006)
items: The right includes: choosing the governing body; appointing teaching and non-teaching staff; admitting eligible students of its choice; fixing a reasonable fee structure; and using its property for the institution.
It also includes the right to teach its children in its own language.

Purpose: to put minorities on equal footing with the majority, not to give them an advantage. So there is no reverse discrimination (favouring minorities over the majority), and general laws still apply.
The right is not absolute; there is no right to maladminister (run the institution badly). The State may set academic standards, staff qualifications, service conditions and syllabus.
Unaided minority institutions may appoint teachers by any rational procedure, subject to State-prescribed qualifications.
Receiving State aid does not take away an institution's minority character, but the State may attach conditions to make sure the aid is used properly.

sections.heading: Who is a minority? Bodies & definitions

items: 'Minority' is not defined anywhere in the Constitution (not even in Art 366, the definitions Article). The Constitution recognises only religious and linguistic minorities.
Even without a definition, Art 30 can still be enforced — the courts decide who is a minority in each case.

Minority status is judged State by State, not for India as a whole (TMA Pai case, 2002). For example, Telugu speakers in Karnataka are a linguistic minority there, and Hindus can be a minority in some States.
Linguistic minority: a group whose mother tongue is different from the majority language of the State or of a part of the State.
National (religious) minorities are notified by the Central Government under the NCM Act 1992: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Parsis (notified in 1993), and Jains (added in 2014).

Benefits of national minority status: the right to run Art 30 institutions, and coverage under the Prime Minister's New 15-Point Programme for minorities. It does NOT give automatic nomination to the Lok Sabha.

Held

rows: Champakam Dorairajan case (1951)
The Madras 'Communal G.O.' (Government Order) that reserved college seats community-wise violated Art 29(2) (and Art 15). A Directive Principle (Art 46) cannot override Fundamental Rights
Led to the 1st Amendment (1951), which inserted Art 15(4)

The Governor reserved the 1957 Kerala Bill for the President, who referred it to the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion under Art 143. The Court held that Art 30 is not absolute — reasonable regulation is allowed
Only the second presidential reference ever made to the Supreme Court

A university may adopt Punjabi as a medium of instruction, but forcing it as the only medium on colleges that must compulsorily affiliate to it violated Art 29(1) and Art 30(1)
Adopting a language is allowed; imposing it is not
Ahmedabad St. Xavier's College case (1974)
State may regulate standards but cannot take away minority's right to administer
Decided by a 9-judge bench on Art 30

Balances Art 29(2) (no discrimination in admission) with Art 30(1) (minority right)

Leading case on Art 30

The State cannot force its reservation quota on unaided institutions, whether minority or non-minority. The State may regulate to stop profiteering and capitation fees

Summarised the principles of Art 30 (see the Art 30 section above)
Scope of right

Upheld the Right to Education (RTE) Act, including its 25% quota in unaided non-minority schools (the quota does not apply to unaided minority schools)
RTE validity

Minority schools are exempt from the RTE Act. In September 2025 (Anjuman Ishaat-e-Taleem Trust case), a 2-judge bench doubted this ruling and referred it to a larger bench (still pending)

blocks.title: Education across the Constitution
items: Many other parts of the Constitution also deal with education: Directive Principles (Art 45 and Art 46); local bodies (11th and 12th Schedules); the Fifth and Sixth Schedules (scheduled and tribal areas); and the Seventh Schedule (education is in the Concurrent List).

Right to Education (RTE) Act 2009: private unaided (non-minority) schools must reserve 25% of seats for children from weaker and disadvantaged groups. The Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) is held by both the Centre (as CTET) and the States — it is not a Centre-only test.
The Constituent Assembly set up the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas (chaired by Sardar Patel) by a resolution of 24 January 1947.

blocks.text: See Right to Freedom for Art 21A

items: Art 29 protects any section of citizens (even the majority); Art 30 protects only religious and linguistic minorities.
Art 29(2) grounds are only religion, race, caste and language — 'sex' and 'place of birth' are not included.
'Minority' is not defined in the Constitution or the NCM Act. The Central Government notifies national minorities. The NCM is a statutory body, not a constitutional one.
Minority status is decided State-wise (TMA Pai case, 2002), not on an all-India basis by the Supreme Court or Parliament.
Art 30(1A) was added by the 44th Amendment, 1978; Art 350A and Art 350B were added by the 7th Amendment, 1956.
Minority rights are not absolute: the State can set standards, there is no right to maladminister, and taking aid does not end minority character.
St Stephen's case: an aided minority institution may give preference to its own community for up to 50% of seats.
Protection of minorities' interests comes under Art 29 and Art 30 (Cultural and Educational Rights), not under Right against Exploitation (Art 23 and Art 24).

subcards.title: Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32) & Writs
subcards.summary: When a Fundamental Right is violated, you can go directly to the Supreme Court (under Art 32) or to a High Court (under Art 226). These courts protect the right by issuing orders called writs; the Constitution names five of them.
at_a_glance: Art 32 is in Part III (Fundamental Rights). The High Courts' writ power is in Art 226, in Part VI.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar called Art 32 'the very soul … and the very heart' of the Constitution
Original (you go to the Supreme Court directly, not by appeal), but not exclusive: High Courts share this power (concurrent jurisdiction)
Art 32: only Fundamental Rights. Art 226 (High Courts): Fundamental Rights and also any other legal right
Habeas corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo warranto
Borrowed from English law, where they were called 'prerogative writs' (writs issued in the King's name)
Part of the basic structure of the Constitution, so it cannot be taken away even by a constitutional amendment
Can be suspended only by an order of the President under Art 359, during a National Emergency

blocks.title: Four clauses of Art 32
head: Clause
Provision
rows: The right to approach the Supreme Court, through proper proceedings, to enforce the rights in Part III is guaranteed. So the remedy itself is a Fundamental Right.
The Supreme Court can issue directions, orders or writs, including the five named writs. Its power is not limited to these five writs.

Parliament may make a law giving any other court the power to issue writs within its local area, without reducing the Supreme Court's power. Only Parliament can do this, not a State legislature and not the Supreme Court through its rules. 'Other court' does not include High Courts, because they already have writ power under Art 226. Parliament has not made any such law so far.
This right cannot be suspended except as the Constitution itself provides, that is, by a President's order under Art 359 during a National Emergency.

blocks.title: Must-know points
items: Ambedkar said: 'an Article without which this constitution would be a nullity. It is the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'. So in exams, 'heart and soul of the Constitution' means Art 32, the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
The Supreme Court is called the 'defender and guarantor' of Fundamental Rights. The judiciary as a whole guards Fundamental Rights through Art 32 (Supreme Court) and Art 226 (High Courts).
The jurisdiction is original: a person goes directly to the Supreme Court, not through an appeal from a lower court. It is also wide: the Court can issue orders, directions and writs of all kinds.
Purpose: to give a remedy that is guaranteed, effective, quick (expeditious), inexpensive and summary (decided without long, formal procedure).

A violation of a Fundamental Right is the sine qua non (essential condition) for Art 32. So Art 32 cannot be used to enforce: constitutional rights that are not Fundamental Rights (for example, the right to property under Art 300A); rights given by ordinary laws (statutory rights) or by custom; or Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs), which Art 37 says no court can enforce.

Having another remedy available does not stop a person from using Art 32. But the Supreme Court has ruled that where relief is available from a High Court under Art 226, the person should approach the High Court first.

The Supreme Court held that Art 32 is a basic feature of the Constitution (Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union case (1981)). Art 32 can still be amended under Art 368 by a special majority (two-thirds), without approval (ratification) by the States — but it cannot be abolished (abrogated).

History: in 1947 the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee of the Constituent Assembly divided its list into two parts. For Part I (justiciable rights, which courts can enforce) it proposed a guaranteed right to approach the Supreme Court. Part II (policy principles) was non-justiciable (courts cannot enforce it).
Before 1950, only the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras could issue writs. Now Art 226 gives this power to all High Courts.

head: Writ
Literal meaning
What it does
Lies against
Not issued
rows: Habeas corpus
'To have the body of'

The person or authority holding someone (the detainer) must bring the detained person before the court. The court examines the reason for and legality of the detention, and frees the person if it is illegal. It is called the 'bulwark (strong defence) of individual liberty'.
Both public authorities AND private individuals
When the detention is lawful; when the detention is for contempt of a legislature or a court; when a competent court ordered the detention; when the detention is outside the court's jurisdiction
Mandamus
'We command'
Commands a public official to perform an official duty (a public duty or one given by law) that he has failed or refused to do. It directs someone to act.
A public official, public body, corporation, lower (inferior) court, tribunal or the government

A private individual or private body; departmental instructions that have no backing of law; a discretionary duty (where the authority may choose); a duty arising only from a contract; the President or State Governors
Prohibition
'To forbid'

A higher court stops a lower court or tribunal from going beyond its jurisdiction or taking a jurisdiction it does not have. It directs someone to stop acting. It only prevents; it does not correct an order already passed.
Only judicial and quasi-judicial authorities (bodies that decide disputes like a court)
Administrative authorities; legislatures; private persons
Certiorari
'To be certified' or 'to be informed'

A higher court calls for the records of a case and cancels (quashes) an order that was passed without jurisdiction, beyond jurisdiction, or with an obvious (patent) error of law. It both prevents and corrects (preventive and curative).
Judicial and quasi-judicial authorities; later also administrative authorities whose actions affect the rights of individuals
Legislative bodies; private individuals
Quo warranto
'By what authority or warrant'
The court enquires whether a person's claim to hold a public office is legal. It prevents someone from illegally occupying (usurping) a public office.
The holder of a substantive public office of a permanent nature, created by a law (statute) or by the Constitution
A ministerial office (one that only carries out orders); a private office
blocks.note: All five writs are named in Art 32(2) and Art 226. They are borrowed from English law, where they were called 'prerogative writs' because they were issued under the special power (prerogative) of the King, seen as the 'fountain of justice'.

blocks.title: Who can apply
items: Normally only the person whose right is affected (the aggrieved person) can apply. This is called locus standi (the right to approach the court).

Habeas corpus: a relative or a genuine (bona fide) friend may file for a detained person who cannot approach the court himself. The petition is not dismissed just because it is badly drafted (imperfect pleadings). It protects all persons, not only citizens.
Quo warranto: any public-minded person may apply. He need not be personally affected and need not claim the office for himself.

blocks.title: Mandamus — limits and reach
items: Mandamus enforces a public duty or a duty given by law that already exists. It cannot force Parliament or a State legislature to make a law (there is no mandamus to legislate).
Once the government has laid down a policy, its terms can be enforced by mandamus. Mandamus cannot be issued where there is no duty or policy.
Discretionary matters: the court can direct an authority to consider the matter and use its discretion lawfully, but the court does not give the benefit itself (CAG v K.S. Jagannathan case (1986)).

Mandamus can be issued against a government company or corporation, because it is a public body. It can be issued against a private body only if that body performs a public duty and the dispute is about that duty (Andi Mukta Sadguru Trust case (1989)). Being private does not by itself protect a body from mandamus.
Mandamus cannot be issued against a judge or Chief Justice acting in a judicial capacity. It can also direct an official not to enforce an unconstitutional law.
Mandamus is not limited to violations of Fundamental Rights; it can also enforce a duty given by an ordinary law (statutory duty).

blocks.title: Details of Habeas corpus, Certiorari and Quo warranto
items: Habeas corpus tests whether the custody is legal. It is not an appeal against a valid conviction by a competent court.
In habeas corpus, the detained person need not always be physically brought before the court (Kanu Sanyal case (1973)).
Certiorari is supervisory, not an appeal. The court does not re-examine the evidence just because another view is possible (T.C. Basappa case (1954)).
Judicial orders of civil courts cannot be challenged by certiorari under Art 226. The High Court supervises such orders under Art 227 instead (Radhey Shyam v Chhabi Nath (2015)).

Quo warranto can be issued when the office holder lacks a required qualification or was appointed in breach of the appointment rules — not on the ground that someone else is more meritorious. If it succeeds, the wrongful holder is removed, but the petitioner is not appointed in his place.

Even if a law provides an appeal, a person can still approach the High Court under Art 226 in some situations — for example, breach of natural justice (fair hearing), lack of jurisdiction, or enforcement of a Fundamental Right (Whirlpool Corporation case (1998)). Relief is still at the court's discretion.

items: PIL began in the USA in the 1960s and in India in the early 1980s. Its pioneers in India were Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati. It is a result of judicial activism (courts taking an active role to protect rights).
PIL is also called Social Action Litigation (SAL), Social Interest Litigation, or Class Action Litigation.

PIL is based on relaxed locus standi (the rule on who may approach the court). Any public-spirited person or organisation with 'sufficient interest' may approach the court on behalf of people who cannot do so themselves because of poverty or disadvantage. The petitioner need not have suffered any personal loss.
A PIL is filed under Art 32 (in the Supreme Court) or Art 226 (in a High Court). In a High Court it is not limited to Fundamental Rights; other legal rights can also be raised.

Epistolary jurisdiction (letter-based jurisdiction): the court treats a letter or telegram as a writ petition. Example: Sunil Batra (II) case (1980), where a Tihar Jail prisoner's letter about the torture of a fellow prisoner was treated as a petition.
Related provisions: Art 39A (free legal aid); Section 133 of the CrPC (now Section 152 of the BNSS), which gives a Magistrate power to remove a public nuisance.

The court checks the petitioner's credentials, whether the case looks correct at first sight (prima facie), and whether there is real public interest. Misuse of PIL — called 'publicity interest', 'private interest', 'paisa interest' or 'politics interest' litigation — is dismissed with costs (a fine).

subcards.title: Art 33–35 & suspension of FRs
subcards.summary: How Fundamental Rights (FRs) can be limited for the armed forces (Art 33), in areas under martial law (Art 34), by laws only Parliament can make (Art 35), and suspended during a National Emergency (Art 358 and Art 359).
at_a_glance: Only Parliament — not State Legislatures, not the President, not the Prime Minister
Parliament can restrict or remove the FRs of the armed forces, police, intelligence agencies and their telecommunication staff
Parliament can pass a law giving indemnity (legal protection from being sued or punished) for acts done under martial law, and can make valid the sentences passed under it
Laws on certain FR matters can be made only by Parliament, so that they are the same across India
Art 19 is suspended automatically — but only when Emergency is declared on the ground of war or external aggression
A President's order suspends the right to go to court to enforce FRs — but Art 20 and Art 21 can never be suspended
Suspension of FRs during Emergency was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany

items: Only Parliament (not State Legislatures) may, by making a law, restrict or abrogate (completely take away) the Fundamental Rights in Part III
Purpose: so that these forces perform their duties properly and discipline is maintained among them

blocks.title: Courts martial & tribunals
items: A law made under Art 33 can exclude courts martial (military courts that try members of the armed forces) from the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts — that is, their decisions cannot be challenged through a writ for enforcing FRs

Decisions of the Armed Forces Tribunal can still be reviewed by a High Court under Art 226, but High Courts should use this power sparingly (rarely and with care) — held by the Supreme Court in Union of India v Parashotam Dass (2023)
Art 34 deals with restrictions on FRs while martial law is in force in any area of India
Parliament may make a law to indemnify (protect from legal action) any government servant OR any other person for acts done to maintain or restore order in that area
Parliament may also validate (make legally valid) any sentence passed, punishment given or forfeiture (taking away of property) ordered under martial law in that area
Such an Indemnity Act cannot be challenged in court for violating FRs. The protection is not automatic — Parliament must actually pass a law
Martial law means 'military rule' (the army takes over governance of an area). The idea comes from English common law. The word is not defined anywhere in the Constitution
The Constitution has no express (written) provision for declaring martial law — it is only implied in Art 34
The Supreme Court has held that declaring martial law does not by itself (ipso facto) suspend the writ of habeas corpus (the court order to produce a detained person before the court)

Martial law is different from (1) military law, which is the law that governs the armed forces themselves, and (2) 'aid to civil power', where the army only helps while the civil government keeps functioning (Entry 2A of the Union List)
